analytic.title: Petri Net-Based Real-Time Scheduling of Time-Constrained Single-Arm Cluster Tools with Activity Time Variation

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: It is challenging to schedule time-constrained cluster tools subject to activity time variation. With the help of their Petri net model, a real-time control policy is used to offset the activity time variation. Based on it, the schedulability conditions and scheduling algorithms are presented for single-arm cluster tools. The schedulability conditions can be analytically checked. Algorithms are developed based on analytical expressions such that it is also computationally efficient. The schedule obtained by the scheduling algorithms together with a real-time control policy forms the real-time schedule. It is optimal in terms of cycle time.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: n semiconductor manufacturing, cluster tools are increasingly adopted. Each of them is composed of several processing modules (PM), an aligner, a wafer handing robot, and two loadlocks for wafer cassette loading/ unloading. The robot can be a single or dual-arm one.

Extensive studies have been conducted in modeling and performance evaluation of cluster tools without considering wafer residency time constraints [1] - [4]. With these studies, periodical scheduling methods are developed. It is shown that, backward scheduling is optimal for single-arm cluster tools if there are no wafer residency time constraints [5] [6].

By considering wafer residency time constraints, studies are made and approaches are presented to find the optimal periodical schedule for dual-arm cluster tools in [7] -[9]. Closed-form solutions are developed to find the optimal periodic schedule for both single and dual-arm cluster tools in [10] [11]. These studies are conducted under deterministic activity time. However, in practice, some abnormal events can take place and schedulability of cluster tools is analyzed in [14]. However, the schedulability condition is shown to be conservative in [12]. By considering bounded activity time variation as well, a real-time control policy is presented to offset the effect of activity time variation as much as possible [12]. Based on the policy, it analyzes the effect of activity time variation on the wafer sojourn time delay in a PM. Then, Manuscript

based on the result, a closed-form scheduling algorithm is proposed to find the optimal schedule for dual-arm cluster tools [13]. The results are applicable for dual-arm cluster tools only under a swap strategy. For single-arm cluster tools, swapping is impossible and the result for dual-arm cluster tools is not applicable. Thus, by following the idea in [12], a real-time control policy is proposed for single-arm cluster tools in [15]. With it, the effect of activity time variation on the wafer sojourn time delay in a PM is analyzed by establishing the upper bound of wafer sojourn time delay. This paper studies the real-time scheduling problem of single-arm cluster tools with wafer residency time constraint and bounded activity time variation, and closed-form algorithms are presented to find the optimal solution.

In the next section, the Petri Net (PN) model and a real-time control policy in [15] are introduced. With them, we present the schedulability conditions and scheduling algorithms in Section 3. An example is used to show the application of the proposed approach in Section 4. Finally, conclusions are presented in Section 5.

div.head: II. PETRI NET MODELING AND REAL-TIME CONTROL POLICY
div.p: A. PN Modeling [16]- [20] A Petri net (PN) is a kind of finite capacity PN = (P, T, I, O, M, K) with K(p) denoting the capacity of place p. A wafer flow pattern for cluster tools can be denoted as (m 1 , m 2 , …, m n ), where n is the number of steps for processing the wafer and m i is the number of PMs used to process the wafers for Step i. In the PN model, place p i is used to model the PMs for Step i with K(p i ) = m i . The loadlocks are treated just as a processing step, called Step 0, and are modeled by p 0 with K(p 0 ) = ∞. Let Ω = {0, 1, …, n} be the set of steps including

Step 0 and ℕ n = {1, …, n} be the set of wafer processing steps. The robot is modeled by place r with K(r) = 1 indicating that it has only one arm. When there is a token in r it implies that the robot arm is available for delivering a wafer. A token in place p i means that a wafer is being processed at a PM modeled by p i . In the paper, a token means a wafer and vice versa when no confusion arises.

For the scheduling of a cluster tool with wafer residency time constraints, it is very important to determine and model if the robot should have a wait before or after performing a task. In PN, two types of robot wait are used: scheduled and unscheduled one. The robot wait should be used to balance the workload among the steps and offset the activity time variation as much as possible. To balance the workload, the robot can wait before unloading a wafer from or loading a wafer to a step [10]. We use place q i1 to model the scheduled robot wait before loading a wafer to Step i, while q i2 the scheduled robot wait before unloading a wafer from Step i. Place q i3 is used to model such an unscheduled robot wait at Step i. Noticed that, places p i , q i1 , q i2 , and q i3 are all timed places. Fig. 2.1. The PN model for system with n steps.

All the transitions in the model are timed transitions too. Transition s i1 models the loading of a wafer into a PM at Step i modeled by p i for processing, and s 01 models the loading of a completed wafer into a loadlock modeled by p 0 . Transition s i2 , i∈ℕ n-1 , models the robot tasks of unloading a wafer from a PM at p i and moving to p i+1 . Transition s 02 models the robot tasks of unloading a wafer from a loadlock at p 0 and moving to p 1 . Transition s n2 models robot tasks of unloading a wafer from p n and moving to a loadlock. Transitions y i1 , i = 0, 1, …, n-2, represent that the robot moves from p i+2 to p i without carrying a wafer. Transitions y (n-1)1 and y n1 represent that the robot moves from p 0 to p n-1 and p 1 to p n , respectively.
Pictorially, p i 's and q ij 's are denoted by , and r is denoted by . Then, the PN model for a system with n steps is shown in Fig. 2.1.

At most of time, a tool operates in the steady state in a periodical way. In this paper, we address the periodical scheduling problem, which involves only the steady state. Thus, we need to model the steady state only. Because a robot task's time is much shorter than a wafer process's time, when the system reaches its maximal production rate in the steady state, there are ∑ = n i i m 1 wafers being concurrently processed. This implies that m i wafers are in processing at step i, i∈ℕ n . Thus, without loss of generality, we let M 0 (p i ) = m i , i ∈ℕ n , meaning that each PM is processing a wafer, M 0 (r) = 1 to indicate that the robot is idle, and M 0 (p 0 ) = n to indicate that there are always wafers to be processed. The PN model shown above is deadlock-prone. For example, when a marking M is reached such that M(p i ) = m i , i ∈ℕ n and M 0 (r) = 1. At this marking, y 01 is enabled and can fire. However, firing y 01 makes the PN dead. Thus, in order to avoid deadlocks in it, a control policy can be introduced to make it live as done in [10].

div.p: Up to now, we have completed the schedulability analysis and presented schedulability conditions. These conditions can be analytically checked. Hence, it is computationally efficient. Each algorithm is formed by a number of analytical expressions and thus it is efficient. Besides the schedulability and scheduling algorithms, an important issue is the schedule's optimality. Then, we have the following theorem.
Theorem 3.5: A schedule obtained by Algorithms 3.1 -3.4 is optimal in terms of cycle time.

Let θ ij be the time taken in real-time for the completion of a wafer at Step i in cycle j, and ψ j be the time taken for the robot in cycle j. Further, let κ j = max i, j {θ ij , ψ j }. According to RCP, the time taken in cycle j must be κ j by operating the system online. If θ ij = κ j , it means that Step i is the bottleneck of the system in cycle j, and if ψ j = κ j , the robot is the bottleneck. Thus, the maximal production rate of the system in cycle j is 1/κ j . This implies that the real-time schedule is optimal.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: When time-constrained cluster tools are subject to the activity time variation, it is challenging to schedule them. Based on the PN model and the wafer sojourn time delay analysis presented in [14], this paper presents the schedulability conditions and scheduling algorithms to obtain a feasible schedule if the system is schedulable. The schedulability conditions are checked via analytical expressions. If they are satisfied, an off-line schedule can be found by using analytical expressions as well. Furthermore, this schedule is optimal in terms of cycle time. This is a significant advance in cluster tool scheduling. For some wafer processing processes, it requires revisiting some PMs. This work assumes that a cluster tool is operated without such wafer revisiting. Thus, it is our future research work to deal with this problem.
